chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 431 to 440, Peyanar's mullai decade on the beauty of the forest (புறவணிப் பத்து): each poem opens 'good indeed is the road my lover took' and adds one more grace of the rainy season on it, peacocks, konrai-crowned men, rain-met forest, doe and fawn, neythal, konrai and kurunthu, mullai after hail, flowering bushes, herders' hamlets, thondri and thalavam, while the woman who says it waits at home.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover has gone and the woman, waiting, dwells on the road he took

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; read from the decade's refrain, in which a woman waiting through the rains praises the road her lover took; the friend comforting her is the other possible speaker

431.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took, she says: up on the dark rock of lovely hue it has even peacocks whose bodies are the colour of sapphire.
431.nuance: Every poem of the decade repeats the same first line and ends on உடைத்தே ('it has... too'), so the praise is cumulative: each poem adds one more beauty of the rainy road. Whether the praise is comfort (the road is safe and the season he promised has come) or a reproach (the road is so lovely it keeps him) the refrain does not say; the peacock on the rock belongs to the hills, not the mullai scrub.

432.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: it has even warriors crowned with konrai like heated gold, looking like men entering a wedding house.
432.nuance: The konrai that crowns the men is the rainy season's flower, so the road shows the season even on its people; கடி may be the wedding or a guarded house, and on the first reading the men look festive as if going to a marriage, a hint of the union the season should bring.

433.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: it has even a forest that has met the rains of the season, which the clouds fling down as water.
433.nuance: கார் is named outright: the season the lover would have promised for his return is on his road, so the praise doubles as notice that the time has come.

iraicchi.act: the doe, with her fawn beside her, frolics in the newly rained land
iraicchi.sense: a mother and young at play together on his road set before the absent man the home and family he should be back with in this season

434.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: where the doe with her fawn leaps about, it has even the joy of the cool rain that has poured down.
434.nuance: The doe is kept with her fawn (மறியுடை), not with a stag; the joy named in line 3 is the creatures' joy, which the waiting woman does not share.

435.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: while the neythal that adorns the ground blooms, it has even konrai bright as golden jewels, and pidavam.
435.nuance: The neythal is a flower of the shore pools set among mullai flowers: the rain has filled the low ground so that a water flower adorns the land itself.

437.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: after cool rain with hailstones has poured, it has even mullai blooming white.
437.nuance: The flower that names the landscape appears in its own decade only here: the road has become fully mullai, the land of waiting.

438.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: with many flowers opening on the green bushes, it has even every quality fit to give delight.
438.nuance: Here the list gives way to a summary (இன்புறத் தகுந பண்பு): the road is fit for joy, and the joy she names is one she does not have.

439.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: it has even hamlets standing in great coolness, where the herders wear garlands of kurunthu.
439.nuance: The herders are settled in cool hamlets for the rains, men at home in the season when the lover is away; the poem does not draw this out, so it is left as scene.

440.reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: at the time the cool rain has granted, it has even thondri bright as flame, and thalavam.

links.note: Both set peacocks in their finery and the konrai-lovely forest of the rains before a waiting woman; Kar Narpathu's friend names the season the cure (மருந்து) for her pallor.
links.teaches: Kar Narpathu spells out that the season's beauty is a promise of return and so a cure, while Ainkurunuru only calls his road good for having it, so the decade's bare praise of the road is the same reassurance left unspoken.

links.note: Both see the konrai as gold (Kuruntokai: பொன்செய் புனையிழை; Ainkurunuru: சுடுபொன் அன்ன கொன்றை); Kuruntokai's heroine refuses the forest's word that the rains have come, since he does not lie.
links.teaches: The gold konrai that Kuruntokai's woman must deny, because admitting the season means admitting a broken promise, is here worn by men on his road and praised, so the same flower could be held off as false witness or welcomed as the season's adornment of his way.

links.note: Kuruntokai's friend calls the konrai foolish for taking a stray shower for the kaar rains (வம்ப மாரியைக் காரென); Ainkurunuru calls the forest on his road one that has met the kaar rain (கார்ப்பெயற்கு எதிரிய).
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows that whether the forest's flowering marks the true kaar was itself what the waiting woman and her friend argued over, Kuruntokai explaining the signs away while Ainkurunuru accepts them.

links.note: Both put a doe with her frisking fawn on the rainy mullai road (Ainkurunuru: மறியுடை மான்பிணை; Akananuru: மறிஆடு மருங்கின் மடப்பிணை); in Akananuru the stag feeds and guards her and the returning man hurries his chariot home.
links.teaches: The image the waiting woman sets on his road without comment is, in Akananuru, the very sight that turns the man homeward, so the doe and fawn worked as a shared sign that the rains call the traveller back to wife and child.

links.note: Both list the flowers of the first rains (Ainkurunuru: தோன்றி, தளவம்; Natrinai: பிடவம், தளவம், கொன்றை, காயா); in Natrinai the returning man sees them and tells his charioteer the kaar has begun.
links.teaches: What the woman praises as the beauty of his road Natrinai shows from the other end, the man reading those same flowers as his deadline and driving hard, so her praise rests on a hope the hero's poem shows being kept.
